name: dijon vinaigrette
instructions:
The workhorse french vinaigrette. CORE IS FOUR INGREDIENTS: garlic + vinegar + olive oil + dijon mustard. Everything else is an enhancer layered on top.

=== CORE ===

- 1 clove garlic (microplaned or crushed)
- vinegar — RED WINE, WHITE WINE, or SHERRY vinegar all work (see VINEGAR CHOICE note)
- olive oil (~3:1 oil to vinegar, adjust to taste)
- dijon mustard (emulsifier + flavor backbone)

=== ENHANCERS (ANY OR NONE) ===

- shallots (minced, macerated with the garlic)
- honey (small squeeze — rounds the acid)
- fresh thyme (small pinch of leaves)
- freshly cracked black pepper
- salt
- warm water (a splash — loosens a too-thick emulsion and mellows the bite)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. MACERATE: microplane or crush the garlic into the vinegar (plus minced shallots if using). Let sit ~15 minutes to soften the raw allium edge and pre-load the vinegar with flavor.
2. BUILD: whisk in the dijon mustard (plus honey and thyme if using). Then slowly drizzle in the olive oil while whisking to emulsify. Ratio roughly 3:1 oil to vinegar; adjust to taste.
3. FINISH: salt and pepper to taste if using. If the emulsion is too thick or too sharp, whisk in a splash of warm water.
notes:
The bare-bones dijon vinaigrette — the workhorse of the vinaigrette family. Renamed from 'basic red vinaigrette' because the DIJON is the identity (emulsifier + backbone) and the vinegar slot is flexible (red wine, white wine, or sherry — not just red).

=== CORE vs ENHANCERS — THE STRUCTURE ===

The four-ingredient core (garlic + vinegar + olive oil + dijon) is a complete dressing on its own. The enhancer list (shallots, honey, thyme, pepper, salt, warm water) is exactly that — enhancements, any or none, chosen per batch:

- SHALLOTS: minced and macerated alongside the garlic. Adds a sweeter, rounder allium layer under the garlic's sharpness. The most common upgrade.
- HONEY: a small squeeze rounds the vinegar's acid. Push toward this when the dressing is going on bitter greens.
- FRESH THYME: small pinch of leaves. Herbal-woodsy note that reads distinctly french.
- BLACK PEPPER + SALT: season to taste; the dijon and vinegar carry enough that some batches don't need either.
- WARM WATER: a splash loosens a too-thick emulsion and mellows an over-sharp batch. SAMIN NOSRAT reportedly calls warm water the SECRET INGREDIENT of a good vinaigrette — it softens the acid's aggression and relaxes the emulsion into something that coats rather than clings, without diluting flavor the way more oil would. Not just a rescue tool; worth adding deliberately.

=== VINEGAR CHOICE — RED WINE, WHITE WINE, OR SHERRY ===

All three work in the vinegar slot:
- RED WINE VINEGAR: the classic. Tannic, structured, most assertive.
- WHITE WINE VINEGAR: lighter, cleaner — better on delicate lettuces.
- SHERRY VINEGAR: the spanish upgrade — nutty-oxidative depth, arguably the best of the three when you have it.

=== MACERATE THE GARLIC — SAME REASON AS ELSEWHERE IN THE VINAIGRETTE FAMILY ===

Raw microplaned garlic is aggressive; the 15-minute sit in the vinegar tames it and infuses the vinegar with garlic flavor. Don't skip. Shallots (if using) macerate in the same bath.

=== DIJON DOES DOUBLE DUTY — EMULSIFIER + FLAVOR ===

Dijon is what makes this an actual emulsified vinaigrette rather than an oil-and-vinegar drizzle. The mustard binds the oil and vinegar so the dressing coats greens evenly instead of separating on the plate. It also adds a sharp savory backbone that keeps the dressing from reading one-note-vinegary.

=== RATIO IS TO TASTE — CLASSIC 3:1 OIL TO VINEGAR IS THE STARTING POINT ===

Some batches want more vinegar (going on assertive greens), some want more oil (going on delicate lettuces). Start at 3:1, taste, adjust. Dijon amount is also to taste — heavier gives you a sharper more mustard-forward dressing, lighter lets the vinegar and garlic lead.

=== WANT TO TRY — HERBES DE PROVENCE ===

Herbes de provence in place of (or alongside) the thyme enhancer. The blend's lavender-sage-thyme character would push the dressing more distinctly provençal. Untested.

=== SIBLING VINAIGRETTES ===

- ketchup-vinaigrette: this dressing + ketchup + dill, pushed into american-cookout register.
- tomato-vinaigrette: red wine + balsamic + macerated shallots/garlic + grated tomato pulp — the italian samin version, no dijon.
- cream-vinaigrette: dairy path (heavy cream + white wine vinegar + raw garlic, no oil).
- strawberry-peach-vinaigrette: the sweet-fruit branch of the samin scaffolding.
- tangerine-mint-vinaigrette: juice-forward, splash-of-vinegar rather than vinegar-forward.
